messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nabil is a 37-year-old firefighter who came to treatment months after a stalking ordeal that had ended on paper but not in his body. He described the beginning of it in fragments rather than a smooth story. A man he had encountered repeatedly around the station and later near his home began appearing in places that should not have overlapped: outside the grocery store, across from the school where his wife worked, beside intersections on a bicycle, waiting just long enough for Nabil to notice him. At first he told himself it was coincidence. What changed things was the growing pattern of being behind him—on foot, in a car mirror, or most vividly, the cyclist trailing him at a measured distance as he drove home after shift. By the time police became involved, Nabil had started taking longer routes and circling blocks to check whether he was being tracked. He remembers the sick certainty of looking up and seeing that bicycle again, close enough to feel deliberate.

Since then, physical locations have become loaded in ways that make immediate sense to him. Pulling into the station parking lot, stopping near the intersection where he used to spot the cyclist, or even entering public buildings with long sightlines can bring the whole memory back without warning. He does not experience it as ordinary remembering. It arrives all at once, with a rush of emotion so strong that he has to cut himself off and focus on something concrete in front of him. When asked to describe exactly what happened over those months, he often says he knows it clearly but cannot find words for it; after a sentence or two, he goes quiet, jaw tight, as if continuing would flood him.

Those moments have changed what he believes about himself. Each time a place or the sense of someone behind him pulls the memory up so forcefully, Nabil thinks, this is not how a solid man reacts. He has come to believe he has permanently changed for the worse since the stalking, and that the intensity of his reactions means he may be going crazy. More than once he said the part he cannot forgive is feeling frightened by something other people might dismiss, which to him proves he is weak. That conclusion has made the triggers feel even more potent: a hallway, a parking lot, the glimpse of a bicycle is no longer just a reminder of what happened, but evidence, in his mind, of what he has become.

At work, this has narrowed his world in ways that embarrass him. As soon as he enters any building, even ones he has been in many times on calls, he scans for exits automatically. Unexpected loud sounds keep him on high alert beyond what he considers normal for the job, and he watches people closely for signs they might harm him, especially anyone lingering near doors or hanging back behind the group. He knows firefighting requires vigilance, but he feels his vigilance has become personal and relentless. Because he believes something in him has broken, he treats every jolt in his body as proof that he cannot trust himself to settle. That belief keeps him keyed up, and the more he remains keyed up, the more convinced he becomes that he is damaged.

The memories and his watchfulness feed each other. When something in the environment abruptly brings back the image of being followed, his body shifts into immediate surveillance: where are the exits, who is near me, who is watching me, what was that sound? Once in that state, every movement around him feels potentially significant. On bad days at the station, if he hears a sudden clang and then notices someone outside near the apparatus bay, his mind leaps back to the stalking before he can slow it down. Later he berates himself for reacting so strongly, telling himself that a stronger man would have shaken this off long ago. Those judgments do not calm him; they make the next memory harder to bear, and they leave him even more convinced that the next place, the next bicycle, the next sensation of someone behind him will undo him again.

Over time he has also begun to enter spaces already braced for the old pattern. If he has to walk from the station lot or cross a downtown block after a call, he is half-expecting to feel tracked, and that expectancy makes ordinary locations feel contaminated before anything has happened. When he does catch sight of a cyclist or senses footsteps behind him, the memory snaps into place so quickly that he feels ambushed by his own surroundings. His wife has noticed that he chooses seats with a view of the door, studies strangers in restaurants, and occasionally cuts outings short without explaining why. At home, he has tried to explain the stalking to her, but when he reaches the parts that matter most, he loses the words and shuts down, which leaves him ashamed and more certain that something fundamental in him has given way.

He sought help after realizing that the problem was beginning to affect his work and marriage in ways he could no longer hide behind discipline. He recently left a family gathering abruptly after hearing a loud noise outside and becoming convinced, for several minutes, that someone was there watching the house. What frightened him most was not only the fear itself but the thought that this might be permanent—that he will keep living as if pursuit is always about to resume, and that his wife will come to know him only as this guarded, scanning version of himself. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to forget what happened but to walk into a room, hear a sound, or see a bicycle without feeling his whole mind and body seized by it.
